1.title: Two Senders, One Church
1.context: Timothy stands in the sender line again, as in 1 Corinthians, where Sosthenes stood instead. The address reaches past the city congregation to all the saints throughout Achaia, the Roman province covering southern Greece.
1.question: Who stands beside your name when you speak to people you love, and what does their presence add?

1.title: The Father of Compassion
1.context: The letter opens with a blessing, as many Jewish prayers did, before any business. Comfort is described as something received in order to be passed on, not stored.
1.question: What comfort have you received that you are now in a position to pass on to someone else?

1.title: Comfort Overflows
1.context: Overflow is the paragraph's governing picture: sufferings overflow to the apostles, and comfort overflows back through Christ to the church. Affliction and comfort are both treated as shared goods.
1.question: Where have you seen someone else's trouble become, unexpectedly, your own comfort?

1.title: The Hardships in Asia
1.context: Asia here is the Roman province in what is now western Turkey, where Ephesus was the capital. The letter never says what the hardship was, and Acts records plots, a riot, and constant danger in the same region without naming this crisis either.
1.question: What has happened to you that you can describe by its effect but still not fully explain?

1.title: The Sentence of Death
1.context: Paul reads his own despair as instruction: the feeling of a death sentence taught reliance on the God who raises the dead rather than on himself.
1.question: What did a season of helplessness teach you about where you actually lean?

1.title: He Will Yet Again Deliver Us
1.context: Past, present, and future deliverance are stacked in one sentence, and the Corinthians' prayers are named as part of the mechanism, with thanksgiving as the intended result.
1.question: Whose prayers for you have you only learned about after the danger passed?

2.title: Our Conscience Testifies
2.context: Boast is a word this letter uses constantly, usually with irony or correction. Here the boast is a clear conscience about conduct, offered as evidence the Corinthians can check against their own experience of him.
2.question: What could your conscience honestly testify about how you have treated the people closest to your work?

2.title: Nothing Beyond Your Ability to Read
2.context: Paul insists his letters contain no hidden second meaning to be decoded by insiders. Boasting of one another in the day of the Lord is pictured as mutual, the church proud of its apostle and the apostle of his church.
2.question: Where are you hoping to be understood completely, by people who now understand you only in part?

2.title: A Double Blessing
2.context: The planned route ran south from Ephesus to Corinth, north to Macedonia, back to Corinth, then east to Judea. A double blessing meant two visits on one journey, which doubled the sting when neither happened.
2.question: What promised good thing of yours failed to happen, and who had to absorb the disappointment?

2.title: Not Yes and No
2.context: The defense rises from travel plans to theology: God's own faithfulness, Christ's consistent yes to the promises, and the church's Amen answering it. Silvanus is Silas, Paul's companion from the second journey.
2.question: Where do people experience your word as yes and no at once, and what would repair it?

2.title: His Seal, His Spirit
2.context: A seal marked ownership and authenticity; a pledge was a first installment guaranteeing the rest. Both pictures describe the Spirit as something already given, not merely awaited.
2.question: What have you already been given that serves as proof of more to come?

2.title: To Spare You
2.context: The reason for the changed plan is sworn with God as witness. Fellow workers is the chosen correction to any picture of apostolic rule: faith stands on its own feet, not under a manager.
2.question: When has staying away been the kindest version of showing up for someone?

3.title: Not Another Painful Visit
3.context: The painful visit is known only from Paul's references to it; Acts narrates the founding visit of Acts 18 and the later stay of Acts 20, but not this one. The letter he wrote instead is likewise known by its effects and his descriptions, and whether it is 1 Corinthians the texts do not say plainly.
3.question: What hard conversation have you put into writing because a room would have made it worse?

3.title: Written Through Many Tears
3.context: Paul describes the letter's composition in bodily terms: distress, anguish of heart, many tears. Its stated purpose was not grief but the proof of love.
3.question: What difficult thing have you had to say to someone precisely because you loved them?

3.title: He Has Grieved All of You
3.context: The offender is never named here, and his exact offense is never stated. The punishment by the majority implies a congregational act, with a minority possibly dissenting.
3.question: How do you respond when a community you belong to has to deal with one of its own?

3.title: Forgive and Comfort Him
3.context: The direction of the church's duty reverses: the same obedience that produced discipline is now asked to produce comfort, before sorrow becomes the whole story.
3.question: Who in your life needs to be reaffirmed in love after a season of being corrected?

3.title: Not Unaware of His Schemes
3.context: Forgiveness is argued for on strategic grounds as well as merciful ones: an unforgiving church hands its adversary an advantage. Forgiven in the presence of Christ frames the act as done before a witness.
3.question: Where might refusing to forgive be costing more than the original wrong did?

4.title: A Door Stood Open
4.context: Troas was the port on the Aegean coast of Asia where ships crossed toward Macedonia. Paul had passed through it on the second journey, when the vision of the Macedonian man redirected him in Acts 16.
4.question: When has a genuinely good opportunity still not been the right one for you to take?

4.title: No Peace in My Spirit
4.context: Titus had been sent to Corinth and was expected back by this route. Paul's restlessness is presented without embarrassment: the apostle left good work undone because he could not bear not knowing how his letter had landed.
4.question: What news are you waiting for that you cannot rest without, and what is the waiting doing to you?

4.title: Led as Captives
4.context: A Roman triumph paraded captives through streets filled with the smoke of incense. Paul casts himself as a captive in Christ's procession, and the fragrance of the procession becomes the knowledge of God spreading everywhere.
4.question: Where has being led, rather than leading, turned out to be your place of honor?

4.title: An Odor, a Fragrance
4.context: One aroma, two verdicts: the picture holds salvation and perishing side by side without resolving the tension. The question about who is qualified is left hanging, and Paul answers it only much later in the letter.
4.question: How do you carry the same message to people who receive it in opposite ways?

4.title: Not Peddlers of the Word
4.context: Peddlers were traders suspected of watering down what they sold. Sincerity and being sent are Paul's counter-claims, themes the defense returns to for the rest of the letter.
4.question: What would it cost you to say plainly that you are not selling anything?

5.title: Letters of Recommendation
5.context: Traveling teachers carried letters from patrons or churches vouching for them. Paul's counter-credential is the congregation itself, publicly readable by everyone.
5.question: If your life were the only letter of recommendation someone could read, what would it say?

5.title: Tablets of Human Hearts
5.context: Stone tablets point to the law given through Moses at Sinai. The contrast is between ink and Spirit, stone and hearts, drawn from the prophets' promises of a law written inside people.
5.question: What has been written on your heart that no external rule could have put there?

5.title: Ministers of a New Covenant
5.context: New covenant language comes from Jeremiah 31. The letter-Spirit contrast has been read in several ways across the church's history; Paul states it as the ground of his competence, which he locates in God rather than himself.
5.question: Where do you need to hear that your competence comes from God rather than from you?

5.title: How Much More Glorious
5.context: The argument runs from lesser to greater: if the old ministry came with glory, the new exceeds it. The glory on Moses' face is called fleeting inside the argument itself, preparing for the veil.
5.question: What good thing in your life has been outshone, not disgraced, by something greater?

5.title: The Veil Remains
5.context: Exodus tells of Moses veiling his fading radiance. Paul reads the veil as still lying over hearts at the reading of the old covenant, removed only by turning to the Lord.
5.question: What do you keep reading, in Scripture or in life, through a veil you have not named?

5.title: Unveiled Faces
5.context: Freedom and transformation close the chapter: unveiled faces reflect glory and are changed by what they behold, with intensifying glory rather than fading.
5.question: What are you beholding regularly enough that it is changing you?

6.title: We Do Not Lose Heart
6.context: Mercy frames the ministry: it was given, not earned. Renouncing secret ways is the ethical signature of a ministry that argues in the open and lets consciences judge it.
6.question: What secret or shameful method have you renounced in your own work, and what did it cost?

6.title: Veiled to Those Who Are Perishing
6.context: The god of this age is Paul's name for the power behind the blindness. The apostles' self-effacement is total: they proclaim Christ as Lord and themselves only as the church's servants.
6.question: Where are you tempted to proclaim yourself when you were sent to proclaim someone else?

6.title: Treasure in Jars of Clay
6.context: The light saying belongs to creation in Genesis 1. Clay jars were the cheapest storage in the ancient world, and the plainness of the container is the point: the power's source must not be confused with its carrier.
6.question: What crack in your own jar has, unexpectedly, let the treasure show?

6.title: Struck Down, Not Destroyed
6.context: Four pairs of blows and survivals, each second line refusing the obvious conclusion. The exchange at the end mirrors chapter 1: death working in the apostles, life in the churches.
6.question: Which of the four pairs describes your present season most exactly?

6.title: I Believed, Therefore I Have Spoken
6.context: The quoted line is Psalm 116:10, a psalm of a man delivered from death who keeps speaking. Resurrection is the ground of the apostles' speech, and grace spreading to more people is its direction.
6.question: What do you keep saying because you believe it, even when saying it costs you?

6.title: An Eternal Weight of Glory
6.context: Light and momentary against eternal weight: the comparison is deliberately out of scale. Seen and unseen are treated as two calendars, one temporary and one not.
6.question: What are you fixing your eyes on that you cannot see, and how does it change what you can?

7.title: An Eternal House
7.context: Tent and building carry the whole contrast: temporary shelter against permanent structure, human hands against God's making. The house is spoken of as already possessed, not merely promised.
7.question: What in your life is a tent, and what has God given that is a building?

7.title: Swallowed Up by Life
7.context: The groaning longs for more covering, not less: clothed, not unclothed. Mortality being swallowed by life reverses the usual direction of swallowing in Scripture, where death does the consuming.
7.question: What do you groan for, exactly, when you are honest about it?

7.title: The Spirit as a Pledge
7.context: Prepared and pledge are both God's verbs here. A pledge is part of the payment already in hand, which is why confidence, rather than anxiety, is the passage's mood.
7.question: What have you already received that guarantees, for you, what is still coming?

7.title: We Walk by Faith
7.context: At home and away are stated as the two addresses of a believer's life, with pleasing him as the ambition that covers both. Walk by faith, not by sight, is the chapter's most quoted sentence and its traveling rule.
7.question: Where are you walking by faith right now because sight is simply not available?

7.title: The Judgment Seat of Christ
7.context: The judgment seat was the raised platform of a Roman official. Paul leaves the sentence unsoftened, addressed to all, and lets it motivate the persuasion of the next episode.
7.question: How does knowing you will give an account change the way you do today's ordinary work?

8.title: We Try to Persuade Men
8.context: Fear of the Lord here is reverence with a courtroom behind it. Paul gives the Corinthians material to answer his critics rather than asking them simply to take his word.
8.question: Whom are you trying to persuade, and what would honest persuasion require of you?

8.title: Christ's Love Compels Us
8.context: Compels pictures pressure from every side, love doing the pressing. One died for all, therefore all died is the conviction from which the new way of regarding people follows.
8.question: Whom do you still regard according to the flesh, by the old measures?

8.title: The New Has Come
8.context: New creation is the passage's headline: in Christ, the old order of a person's life has passed and the new has arrived. Paul immediately traces it to God's initiative in the next scene.
8.question: What old thing has passed away in you, and what new thing are you still learning to notice?

8.title: Ambassadors for Christ
8.context: An ambassador speaks for a ruler in a foreign court. Reconciliation's message is described as committed to the apostles, like funds entrusted to carriers, and the appeal is made to people already in the church.
8.question: Where have you been sent as an ambassador, and whose appeal are you carrying?

8.title: The Righteousness of God
8.context: The exchange is stated without cushioning: the one who knew no sin made sin, so that those in him might become God's righteousness. The verse has anchored centuries of reflection on how the cross works; the letter simply states it.
8.question: What would change if you received this exchange as settled rather than as something to complete?

9.title: Now Is the Day of Salvation
9.context: The quoted promise is Isaiah 49:8, spoken to God's servant. Paul's comment collapses the distance between prophecy and present: the time of favor is now, and grace can still be received in vain.
9.question: What have you been treating as a future day that this passage says is today?

9.title: In Great Endurance
9.context: The commendation of the ministry is a list of conditions endured, not results achieved. Beatings, imprisonments, and riots are the public record; labor, sleepless nights, and hunger are the private one.
9.question: What has your endurance quietly been proving to the people watching you?

9.title: Having Nothing, Possessing Everything
9.context: Character traits and paradoxes complete the catalogue: weapons in both hands, dishonor and praise, poverty that enriches. The pairs refuse to let circumstance have the last word about a life.
9.question: Which paradox in this list is your life currently living out?

9.title: Open Wide Your Hearts
9.context: The appeal narrows from the church's conduct to the church's affections. A fair exchange between a father and his children is the frame: feeling answered with feeling.
9.question: Toward whom has your heart narrowed, and what would opening it cost?

10.title: What Fellowship Has Light With Darkness
10.context: A yoke joins two animals to one load. Belial is an old name for worthlessness used here for the power opposed to Christ. The five questions are rhetorical: each expects the answer, none.
10.question: What partnership in your life pulls against the direction you say you are going?

10.title: The Temple of the Living God
10.context: The stacked promises weave Leviticus 26, Isaiah 52, Ezekiel 37, and 2 Samuel 7. God's dwelling with his people is the ground given for the church's separation, not a reward for it.
10.question: What promise of God's presence do you most need to hear as addressed to you?

10.title: Make Room for Us
10.context: Cleansing and confidence stand side by side: holiness perfected in the fear of God, and an apostle boasting that his pride in this church overflows in all his troubles.
10.question: Who has made room for you in their heart in a way you have not yet thanked them for?

10.title: Comforted by the Arrival of Titus
10.context: Macedonia is where the letter is being written, and this is its moment of origin: Titus arriving with the church's answer. Conflicts outside and fears within are the honest weather report of the apostle's mind.
10.question: Whose arrival, or whose news, has comforted you when you were downcast?

10.title: Godly Sorrow
10.context: Two sorrows are distinguished by their fruit: one leads to repentance and salvation, the other to death. Verse 11 lists the produce of the godly kind like fruit on a tree, ending in vindication.
10.question: What sorrow in your life has led you toward repentance rather than away from God?

10.title: Complete Confidence in You
10.context: The letter's purpose is re-read after the fact: it aimed at the church's earnestness, not at the two men in the case. Titus's refreshed spirit and Paul's vindicated boasting close the long Corinth story of the letter's first half.
10.question: Whose confidence in you has proved true, and how were they proved right?

11.title: The Grace Given the Churches of Macedonia
11.context: The collection was for the poor saints in Jerusalem, and it occupies two full chapters. Macedonia's churches gave from inside a terrible ordeal, joy and deep poverty named in the same sentence.
11.question: What have you seen people give out of their poverty that the comfortable rarely give out of surplus?

11.title: They Pleaded for the Privilege
11.context: The Macedonians' giving was voluntary to the point of begging for inclusion. Paul traces the order: themselves first to the Lord, then to the apostles, which makes the money the second gift, not the first.
11.question: What have you given that only became a real gift after you had given yourself?

11.title: Excel in This Grace
11.context: Titus started the collection at Corinth and returns to complete it. Calling giving a grace, and something to excel in alongside faith and knowledge, is Paul's framing throughout the chapter; the test is earnestness, not amount.
11.question: In which grace have you excelled while quietly neglecting this one?

11.title: He Became Poor
11.context: Christ's riches and poverty measure the appeal, not other churches' totals. The manna rule of Exodus 16 closes the argument: equality pictured as gathered amounts evening out.
11.question: What does according to what one has, not what he does not have, free you to give?

11.title: Right in the Eyes of Men
11.context: Three carriers travel with the gift: Titus and two brothers, one of them chosen by the churches themselves. Administration is treated as part of the ministry's witness, done carefully before two audiences.
11.question: What money or trust in your care needs a second pair of eyes, for everyone's sake?

12.title: I Know Your Eagerness
12.context: Achaia's readiness, boasted about for a year, had already stirred Macedonia to give. The two collection chapters provoke in both directions: each region's zeal is used to encourage the other's.
12.question: Whose example of generosity has stirred you to act on what you already intended?

12.title: Prepared Generously, Not Begrudgingly
12.context: The brothers go ahead so the gift can be arranged before Paul arrives. A promised gift collected under pressure at the door is described as begrudged; preparation is what keeps it generous.
12.question: What promised generosity of yours needs arranging now, before it becomes an embarrassment?

12.title: God Loves a Cheerful Giver
12.context: Sowing and reaping set the scale; the heart's decision sets the amount. Regret and compulsion are the two forbidden motives, and cheerfulness is the quality God is said to love.
12.question: What do you give that you would give more cheerfully if no one ever knew?

12.title: Seed for the Sower
12.context: The quoted line is Psalm 112:9, describing the righteous man's scattered gifts. God's supply is pictured as seed and bread from the same hand, with enrichment aimed at generosity rather than storage.
12.question: What has God supplied to you that was seed for others rather than bread for you?

12.title: His Indescribable Gift
12.context: The gift's destination is traced past the saints' needs to their thanksgiving and prayers for the givers. The chapter's last word, indescribable, turns from the collection to God's own gift, which the appeal has been imitating all along.
12.question: What thanksgiving has your giving produced that you never got to hear about?

13.title: I, Paul, Appeal to You
13.context: At 10:1 the letter's tone changes sharply, from reconciliation to defense, and the telling walks it as the one letter it is. Strongholds here are arguments and presumptions, and the warfare's weapons are declared not fleshly.
13.question: What stronghold of argument in your own thinking needs demolishing rather than decorating?

13.title: Building Up, Not Tearing Down
13.context: Authority is defined by its direction: given for building up. Judging by outward appearances is the error the whole section answers, beginning with whose a person is.
13.question: Where do you judge by outward appearances, in yourself or in others, most readily?

13.title: Weighty and Forceful
13.context: The critics' sentence is the only direct quotation of the opposition in the letter: letters weighty, presence unimpressive, speaking of no account. Paul answers by promising consistency between his words and his arrival.
13.question: What do people say about you at a distance that your presence would need to answer?

13.title: Boast in the Lord
13.context: The assigned field is Paul's measuring rule against self-measuring rivals. The closing rule quotes Jeremiah 9:24, and approval is relocated from self-commendation to the Lord's commendation.
13.question: What field has God assigned you, and where are you tempted to boast beyond it?

13.title: Jealous With a Godly Jealousy
13.context: The betrothal picture casts Paul as the friend who promised the bride. Eve and the serpent bring Genesis 3 into the argument: deception, not force, is the danger named.
13.question: What simple and pure devotion of yours is most at risk of being led astray gradually?

13.title: False Apostles, Masquerading
13.context: Super-apostles is Paul's ironic label, in his quotation marks in the text itself. The free-of-charge preaching, offered as love, had been read at Corinth as worthlessness, and the masquerade language borrows Satan's disguise as an angel of light.
13.question: How do you tell a masquerade from the real thing when both speak the same language?

14.title: Receive Me as a Fool
14.context: Paul flags his own speech as foolishness before and during it: not as the Lord would speak. The irony is aimed at a church that tolerates enslaving teachers while interrogating its founder.
14.question: What true thing about yourself can you only say while apologizing for saying it?

14.title: So Am I
14.context: The pedigree contest ends in a draw, so the comparison moves to service. Servants of Christ is the rivals' claimed title, and Paul's answer is a record they would not want as their own.
14.question: Where are your real credentials written, if not on paper?

14.title: The Forty Lashes Minus One
14.context: Thirty-nine lashes was the synagogue's maximum discipline, given five times. The catalogue that follows has been compared to the hardship lists of ancient philosophers, but its items are mostly unheroic: cold, hunger, sleeplessness, and worry for the churches.
14.question: Which item in Paul's catalogue is closest to a cost you have actually paid?

14.title: Lowered in a Basket
14.context: Aretas was the Nabataean king whose governor watched Damascus. Acts 9 tells the same escape from the narrator's side; Paul's own telling here is the boast he chooses, an undignified exit in a basket.
14.question: What weakness of yours would you boast of, if you boasted the way Paul finally does?

14.title: Caught Up to Paradise
14.context: Fourteen years before this letter, the experience was already old, and Paul tells it in the third person about a man in Christ. What was heard is declared inexpressible and not permitted to be told, and the telling here adds nothing to it.
14.question: What have you experienced that you have learned to hold quietly rather than display?

14.title: A Thorn in My Flesh
14.context: What the thorn was, the letter never says, and readers' guesses across the centuries have never settled it. Messenger of Satan and given stand in the same sentence, and three pleas for removal are the recorded response.
14.question: What have you pleaded with God to remove that he has, so far, left in place?

14.title: My Grace Is Sufficient
14.context: The answer to the three pleas is a sentence, not a removal. Power perfected in weakness becomes the apostle's stated delight, reversing the values of the whole fool's speech.
14.question: Where might God's power be resting on you precisely where you feel weakest?

15.title: Forgive Me This Wrong
15.context: Signs, wonders, and miracles are named as an apostle's marks, performed with perseverance rather than spectacle. The apology for not being a burden is irony, and it lands as the fondest insult in the letter.
15.question: What wrong have you done people mainly by refusing to need them?

15.title: Not Your Possessions, but You
15.context: Parents saving for children is the picture for an apostle who will spend and be spent. The trickery charge is answered with Titus's conduct, since the same accusation had followed the collection's carriers.
15.question: Who has spent themselves for your soul without keeping accounts, and have you thanked them?

15.title: To Build You Up
15.context: The defense is re-labeled at its end: spoken before God, aimed at building up. The fears that follow are pastoral, about the state he will find, and about grief rather than victory if he finds it unchanged.
15.question: What are you afraid you will find, the next time you return to a place you love?

15.title: By the Testimony of Witnesses
15.context: The witnesses rule quotes Deuteronomy 19:15. A third visit frames the whole letter: the first founded the church, the second was painful, and this one is announced with its warning repeated from absence.
15.question: What have you warned about twice that you hope never to have to act on?

15.title: Examine Yourselves
15.context: The demanded test is handed back: examine yourselves. Paul's prayer prefers the Corinthians' rightdoing to his own vindication, even at the price of appearing to have failed himself.
15.question: If you examined yourself as rigorously as you examine others, what would the test show?

15.title: The God of Love and Peace
15.context: The final blessing names Father, Son, and Spirit in the form the church has repeated ever since. It closes a letter that contained the sharpest warnings Paul ever wrote to a church he founded.
15.question: Which line of this farewell do you most need to carry into your week?
